headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when CrewAI processes content-writing outputs from an unisolated prompt-engineering repo.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is a content-writing repo with no runtime surfaces, so it cannot inject by itself. But Profile B has stdin/stdout, files, and shared-memory crew behavior, so if A's content is fed into B as prompts or files, B may treat attacker-controlled text as instructions. The pathway is plausible in default crew workflows, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF Profile A content is ingested by Profile B as prompt text or file content
IF Profile B parses that content without provenance or instruction/data separation
mitigations: Add a strict instruction/data delimiter in the crew prompt template
Prefix all A-derived text with a non-executable provenance tag
Disable automatic file-to-prompt ingestion for the crew
requires-engineering: add provenance tracking for every B input
Run a one-file canary test with benign adversarial text

B_data_leakage.rationale: Profile B reads and writes the host working directory and handles API keys; Profile A is a repository of prompt-engineering material that could be placed in the same workspace. If sensitive crew inputs or secrets land in that shared directory, B can read them and send them to model providers or tools. A itself does not expose data, but the pair creates a shared-workspace leakage path.
conditions: IF Profile A and Profile B share the same host working directory
IF sensitive crew inputs or secrets are stored in files readable by Profile B
mitigations: Move B to a dedicated workspace directory
Store secrets outside the shared directory
Review the crew tool list for any file-uploading steps
Set file permissions to prevent cross-agent reads
requires-engineering: isolate B in a container with a private volume

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Profile A has no write capabilities, while Profile B can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses. There is no direct write-write conflict, but B's broad host access can overwrite or consume files that A's repository content references if both share a directory. Uncertainty remains because A's runtime behavior is undocumented, so the safer medium rating is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same writable directory
IF Profile B writes artifacts that Profile A later reads or publishes
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Disable B writes except to a scratch folder
Avoid concurrent runs against the same repo checkout
Add a lockfile around shared artifacts
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem namespaces

D_cascading_error.rationale: Profile A is a prompt-engineering resource, so its outputs may be treated as guidance or examples by Profile B's crew. Because B supports shared memory and tool execution, A-derived text can become authoritative input unless explicitly verified. That creates a realistic cascade from content to action, though not enough evidence for high severity.
conditions: IF Profile B uses Profile A material as prompts, policies, or task instructions
IF B executes tools based on A-derived text without a verification step
mitigations: Require human review before tool execution
Add a verification step that checks A-derived claims against sources
Mark A content as examples only in the crew prompt
Log every action back to its originating text
requires-engineering: add policy gating before tool calls

E_compliance.rationale: No specific regulated data class, residency mismatch, or certification gap is documented for Profile A. Profile B does handle API keys and developer-passed crew data, but the pairwise compliance risk is limited to generic handling concerns rather than a proven residency or retention violation. I therefore keep this low and do not cite A beyond its open-source/docs-only status.
conditions: IF regulated data is passed into Profile B's crew inputs
IF Profile B's tool integrations retain or transmit that data outside the operator's policy
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in crew inputs
Review provider retention settings before use
Document the data classes allowed in the crew
Rotate any exposed API keys
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls to the deployment
